newsitem.title: UK: Experts worry tobacco companies will turn to poor.
newsitem.headline: Experts worry tobacco companies will turn to poor.

text.p: The admission by a U.S. tobacco company that its cigarettes are addictive will fuel lawsuits in the industrialised world, but will change little for the biggest consumers of tobacco -- developing countries, experts said on Friday.

On Thursday Liggett Group made the astonishing move of admitting that smoking damages health and is addictive. It has agreed to let its employees testify in trials of other tobacco firms and to label its cigarettes with warnings about the hazards of nicotine.
While welcoming the move, health experts were suspicious about its motives and worried about where the tobacco companies would now turn for their profits.
"The tobacco industry will remain a vigorous and profitable enterprise flourishing across the world, leaving death and disease in its wake," said John Moxham of the British Thoracic Society.

"Taking the cynical view, one would imagine that the reason for taking this decision is a damage limitation exercise," agreed Dr David Phillips, a research scientist for the Institute of Cancer Research in London.

"Where it will mostly have effect is in the courts." This would be mostly in the United States, Britain and France, where lawsuits against tobacco companies are pending and, ironically, where tobacco use is dropping.
"Their future markets are increasingly in the third world where there are fewer checks on their activities," Phillips said.

Warnings are required on cigarette packets in industrialised countries like the United States, Britain and Germany, which also restrict cigarette advertising. But developing nations rarely go to such trouble.
The World Health Organisation says on average three million people die each year from smoking-related causes and predicts 10 million will die every year by the 2020s.
Seventy percent of the deaths will be in developing countries, it says.
In the early 1990s, the latest period that WHO has data for, there were 1.1 billion smokers around the world -- 800 million of them in developing countries.

The biggest smokers are the Koreans, according to the WHO. Its survey found that more than 68 percent of Korean men and nearly seven percent of women smoked. Latvia, the Russian Federation, where 30 percent of women also smoke, and the Dominican Republic followed closely.

By far the biggest market is in China, where 61 percent of the men in a nation of 1.2 billion people smoke. "In China alone there are about 300 million smokers, about the same number as in all developed countries combined," WHO said.
As in the industrialised world, it is a habit that starts young. "For example in South Africa, over half of young men under the age of 35 are smokers," WHO says.
The trend in the developed world is downwards.
In France, land of Gauloises and smoky cafes, tobacco consumption has been on a steady decline since 1991, when it peaked at 97.1 billion cigarettes, according to French tobacco company Seita.
The French smoked only 86.2 billion cigarettes in 1996, SEITA said, blaming a growing anti-smoking movement and sharply higher prices -- due primarily to state tax increases.
The WHO, charities and other organisations say governmental control is the key to cutting back smoking figures.
"I renew my call to all political parties to commit themselves now to a complete ban on tobacco advertising and sponsorship," said Sandy Macara, chairman of the British Medical Association.
